what_its_for: This medicine is used to treat severe heart failure. It helps your heart pump blood more effectively by relaxing the blood vessels so your heart does not have to work as hard. It is given in a hospital setting, usually when other heart medicines have not worked well enough.
how_to_take: This medicine is given to you through a vein (IV) by a nurse or doctor in a hospital or clinic. You will not give this medicine to yourself at home in most cases. It is given as a slow, continuous drip through an IV line. Your medical team will carefully monitor your heart rate, blood pressure, and other vital signs while you receive this medicine. Never try to adjust the drip rate yourself.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your weight, kidney function, and how well your heart is working. A starting dose is usually given as a loading dose over about 10 minutes, followed by a continuous lower dose that can last for several hours to several days. The dose may be adjusted by your care team based on how you respond to treatment. Always follow your medical team's instructions.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given continuously by trained medical staff in a hospital, you do not need to worry about missing a dose yourself. If your IV line becomes disconnected or the infusion is interrupted for any reason, alert your nurse or doctor right away so they can restart it safely.
storage: You will not need to store this medicine at home, as it is only given in a hospital or clinical setting. Hospital staff store the premixed bags at controlled room temperature, away from light, and check expiration dates before use. Once a bag is opened and connected to an IV line, it should be used within the timeframe recommended by the hospital pharmacy.
what_to_avoid: While receiving this medicine, avoid getting up too quickly from a lying or sitting position, as it can cause dizziness or a drop in blood pressure. Avoid drinking alcohol. Tell your medical team about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you are taking, because some medicines can interact with milrinone and affect your heart rhythm or blood pressure. Do not take any new medicines without telling your doctor first.
when_to_call_doctor: Tell your nurse or doctor right away if you experience any of the following while receiving this medicine: fast, irregular, or pounding heartbeat or chest pain; sudden dizziness or feeling faint; shortness of breath that gets worse; swelling in your legs or ankles that gets worse; headache or tremors; signs of a low potassium level such as muscle cramps or weakness; pain, redness, or swelling at the IV site; or if you feel something is wrong. Since you are already in a hospital, your care team is nearby to help you.
when_it_works: Milrinone begins working fairly quickly after it is started through your IV. Most patients begin to notice improved breathing and less shortness of breath within the first few hours of treatment. Your medical team will be monitoring your heart and blood pressure to track how well the medicine is working for you.
special_populations: Kidney problems: Your dose will likely be lower if your kidneys are not working well, because this medicine is removed from your body mainly through the kidneys. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to the blood pressure-lowering effects of this medicine and will be monitored closely. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, as the safety of this medicine in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been fully established. Children: This medicine can be used in children with heart failure but must be dosed carefully by a specialist.
